# Welcome {.center}

10:00 - 17:00, three slots with two breaks for lunch and coffee.

---

##

By 17:00 you will have:

- trained a deep model on real EEG,
- watched it fail in two different ways,
- and learned seven strategies for keeping it from failing again.

---

##

A two-year-old learns to recognize a cat from about eight examples.

A standard deep network needs about eight million.

---

## What this lecture is really about

The branch of deep learning that has been quietly trying, for the last decade, to close that gap.

The textbook name for this branch is **learning with fewer labeled examples** — the title and topic of Chapter 19 of the PML book (Murphy 2022).

Today is that chapter, in code, on brain data, reorganized around what resource each strategy exploits.

---

## The problem

You have a model with a million parameters.

You have 30 labeled examples.

What do you do?

::: {.fragment}
The PML book answers this in seven different ways.
:::

# Working with What You Have {.center background-color="#1a1a1a"}

## 10:00 - 12:00 · `01_single.ipynb`

PML 19.1, 19.3, 19.7

---

## Goal

Take **one subject's** EEG and ask: how much can we squeeze out of it?

Train a classifier, watch it fail when labels are scarce, then apply four fixes that all stay **inside the same dataset** — no transfer, no pretraining (that comes after lunch).

---

## Open the notebook

`01_single.ipynb` — Colab badge at the top, or `github.com/ccs-unilu/few2026`.

- Runtime → Change runtime type → **T4 GPU** (needed for §7).
- Run the install cell once: `moabb`, `braindecode`, `pyriemann`, `seaborn`.
- First data download is ~500 MB / ~5 min, then cached.

**Open it now** and let the download run while we talk.

---

## What you need to know: the signal

Imagine clenching your left fist. Without moving. Now your right.

A small, reliable change happens in your sensorimotor cortex: the alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) rhythms over the **contralateral** hemisphere weaken. This is **event-related desynchronization** (ERD).

If we can measure ERD, we can decode which hand you imagined.

---

## What you need to know: the dataset

**PhysioNet Motor Imagery** (Schalk et al. 2004).

- 109 subjects, 64-channel EEG, 160 Hz.
- Each trial: imagined movement of the left or right hand.
- Standard MOABB benchmark; today 10 subjects to keep downloads polite.

The raw trace looks like noise. The notebook's first move is to extract **log bandpower** per channel and band — 64 × 2 = 128 features.

---

## Failure mode 1: not enough labels

Train and test on subject 1, but give the classifier only 5, 10, 20, 40, or 60 trials per class.

The learning curve is monotonic and **steep at the bottom**: with 5 trials per class the model is barely above chance.

This is the **central failure of Ch. 19.** Every fix below is a different way to make the curve climb faster.

---

## Fix 1: Riemannian tangent space

Each trial gives a channel covariance matrix $C_i$. These live on a curved manifold — the cone of symmetric positive-definite matrices, $\mathrm{SPD}(64)$.

Project to a flat tangent space at the geometric mean $\bar C$, then a standard linear classifier can eat them:

$$s_i \;=\; \mathrm{upvec}\!\left(\log\!\big(\bar C^{-1/2}\, C_i\, \bar C^{-1/2}\big)\right)$$

Embarrassingly competitive on motor imagery for over a decade — often beats deep models when labels are very few.

---

## Fix 2: augmentation (PML 19.1)

A trial is one sample from a larger family of acceptable trials. Shift time by 50 ms — still "left hand". Drop an electrode — still "left hand".

Augmentation encodes **invariances** without writing them down. Four one-liners: time shift, channel dropout, Gaussian noise, and **mixup**:

$$\tilde x = \lambda x_i + (1-\lambda)\, x_j, \qquad \lambda \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\alpha)$$

Cog-sci analog: a child concluding that a cat under different lighting is still a cat.

---

## Fix 3: pseudo-labeling (PML 19.3)

The unlabeled trials are still there, and their distribution matches the labeled ones. The simplest semi-supervised move:

1. Train on the small labeled set.
2. Predict on the pool; keep the confident ones, $\max_k p_\theta(k\mid x) \ge \tau$ (here $\tau = 0.85$).
3. Add them to training. Retrain.

Cog-sci analog: a first literature review — read a few papers closely, skim many, trust your judgment on the easy ones. **If your judgment is good this works; if not, it amplifies your bias.**

---

## Fix 4: label smoothing (PML 19.7)

Real labels are messy — we cannot verify what the subject imagined; clinical EEG interrater agreement caps near 80%.

Standard cross-entropy demands "class 1, 100% certain". Label smoothing softens the target:

$$\tilde y_k = (1-\varepsilon)\,[\,k = y\,] + \frac{\varepsilon}{K}, \qquad \mathcal L = -\sum_k \tilde y_k \log p_\theta(k\mid x)$$

With $K=2,\ \varepsilon=0.1$ the target is $(0.9, 0.1)$ — the model never gets infinite gradient pressure to fit a single label. We corrupt 10–30% of labels and watch it degrade gracefully.

---

## Discussion: within-dataset fixes

- Riemannian features from 2012 are still close to state of the art. What does that say about "deep" vs "geometric" representations for EEG?
- Mixup blends two trials and their labels. Does that make biological sense for EEG?
- Pseudo-labeling worked because the unlabeled trials matched the labeled ones. What if the pool came from a different subject?

(Poll on screen.)

---

## Module 1 wrap

- The within-subject few-labels curve is the **diagnosis**; everything else is a fix.
- Better features (Riemannian) and pseudo-labels are the largest wins on this dataset.
- Augmentation buys a few points; label smoothing only earns its keep once labels are actually noisy.
- None of these techniques borrow from anyone else.

**Bridge.** After lunch the classifier still fails — but for a different reason: the wrong person.

## Failure mode 2: not the right person

Same paradigm, different brain. Train on subject 1, test on subject 2, **zero calibration**.

Sweep all 10 subjects in both directions:

- within-subject accuracy: **0.65–0.85**
- cross-subject accuracy: **near 0.55**

That gap is the second failure of Ch. 19. The whole afternoon is about closing it.

---

## The idea: a pretrained model is a prior

Train a small EEGNet on **9 subjects**. It now knows what good EEG features look like — properties of the human sensorimotor system, not of any one person.

The frozen model is the **prior**. Whatever we put on top — a logistic regression, a fine-tuned final layer — is the **posterior update**.

You will recognize this framing from Bayesian cognitive science.

---

## Fix 1: borrowed features (PML 19.2, frozen)

Run three feature extractors on the target subject, train the *same* logistic regression on each:

::: {.list-table}
- - Features
  - Era
  - Cost

- - Bandpower
  - 1990s
  - Trivial

- - Riemannian tangent space
  - 2010s
  - Cheap

- - Pretrained EEGNet penultimate
  - 2020s
  - One forward pass
:::

The pretrained penultimate sits above both hand-engineered baselines. **Borrowing pays even when the network never touches the target.**

---

## Fix 2: transfer learning (PML 19.2)

Four conditions on the same target test set decompose "what does pretraining buy you?":

::: {.list-table}
- - Regime
  - Pretrain
  - Fine-tune

- - From scratch
  - none
  - target only

- - Zero-shot transfer
  - 9 source subjects
  - none

- - Fine-tuned transfer
  - 9 source subjects
  - 20 target trials

- - + augmentation
  - 9 source subjects
  - 20 target + augmented
:::

From scratch is barely above chance; zero-shot is only a little better. Fine-tuning bridges them, augmentation adds a bit more. **The fixes stack.**

---

## Fix 3: few-shot calibration (PML 19.6)

The chronic problem of BCI: every new user needs a 20-minute calibration session. Can we shrink it to one minute?

Sweep $N \in \{1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50\}$ target trials per class, fine-tune the pretrained EEGNet on each, plot the curve.

The shape tells you what "enough calibration" means for *your* application: a research demo lives at the steep part; a wheelchair controller does not.

---

## Cog-sci framing: priors

Lake et al. (2015) made the same argument with humans on Omniglot: people learn from one or a few examples because they bring **strong priors**.

Pretraining on 9 other subjects is that prior. The parameters are borrowed instead of philosophized.

---

## Optional coda: the recipe outside EEG (§7)

A 10-minute detour: "frozen encoder + tiny classifier" is not EEG-specific.

Embed ~40 DSM-5-style sentences with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` (open-weight, T4-friendly), project to 2D with UMAP, watch four clusters emerge with **no supervision**.

Same recipe, different modality.

---

## Discussion: borrowing

- Why is "pretrained on 9 brains" only modestly above chance for motor imagery, when "pretrained on ImageNet" is often enough for natural images?
- If you could keep only one — augmentation or transfer — which, and why?
- Real label noise is often *systematic*. Does any of today's borrowing help with that?

---

## Module 2 wrap

- A frozen pretrained encoder + a simple classifier is the strongest first move in 2026.
- Geometry-aware features (Riemannian) are still hard to beat on small EEG data.
- Fine-tuning + augmentation stack.
- Few-shot calibration turns "20 minutes" into "1 minute" at little accuracy cost.
- The recipe transfers across modalities — same idea works on text.

**Bridge.** Five strategies covered. The last two target a different question: not what to *borrow*, but what to *ask*.

## Active learning (PML 19.4)

You have an unlabeled pool; each label costs something (in BCI, a calibration trial). Which examples should you label first?

The classical answer is **uncertainty sampling**: train on a small seed, then iteratively pick the example the model is least sure about.

$$x^\star = \arg\max_{x\in\mathcal U}\ \big[\,1 - 2\,\lvert p_\theta(x) - 0.5\rvert\,\big]$$

In general, maximize predictive entropy $H(p) = -\sum_k p_k \log p_k$. Confident examples teach nothing; boundary examples teach a lot.

---

## Cog-sci framing: adaptive psychophysics

Uncertainty sampling is exactly what an adaptive psychophysics protocol does.

**QUEST** (Watson & Pelli, 1983), staircase methods, computerized adaptive testing — all special cases of "choose the next observation to maximize expected information gain". PML 19.4 is the formal version.

A skilled clinical interviewer does the same without naming it: the most informative questions are the ones whose answers you cannot predict.

---

## Meta-learning: MAML (PML 19.5)

Pretraining finds one good initialization. **MAML** (Finn et al., 2017) asks for more — an initialization that adapts in a few gradient steps.

Each task $\tau$ is a subject; episodes split into support and query.

$$\theta'_\tau = \theta - \alpha\,\nabla_\theta\,\mathcal L^{\text{supp}}_\tau(\theta)
\qquad
\min_\theta \sum_\tau \mathcal L^{\text{qry}}_\tau(\theta'_\tau)$$

Inner loop adapts; outer loop tunes the initialization so adaptation works. On motor imagery, MAML rarely beats well-tuned pretraining by much — **the mechanism is the point.**

---

## Cog-sci framing: learning sets

"Learning to learn" comes from Harlow's 1949 study of rhesus monkeys.

Monkeys solving many similar discrimination problems got faster at new ones — eventually solving them after a single trial. He called it a **learning set**.

MAML is the modern, gradient-friendly formalization. The hierarchical-Bayes view makes it explicit: what is learned across tasks is a **prior over weights**, which functions as the learning set.

---

## Discussion: smarter strategies

- A colleague hands you a PhD dataset of 30 EEG trials. Which of the day's strategies do you reach for first? Why?
- Several methods (pseudo-labeling, MAML, augmentation) amplify whatever assumptions the model already had. When is that good, when dangerous?
- Pick one cognitive analog we invoked today and argue that it is *misleading* rather than helpful.

---

## Module 3 wrap

- Active learning is adaptive experimental design with a loss function.
- Choosing *what* to label is often more useful than labeling more.
- Meta-learning is the formal version of "learning to learn".
- Every section of PML Ch. 19 now has a result on the same EEG dataset.
